-to state that, "He did it again".
Then I refer to Anglo-American unity, and in that connection to the article by Mr. Leslie Howard who mentioned the vision of the new world order which the Canadian Prime Minister and other leaders of the British peoples have had such a part in bringing about. Lord Beaverbrook in his broadcast on Sunday, March 23, gave direct credit to the Prime Minister of Canada for the close collaboration between the United States and Britain as one of the crowning achievements in connection with the war. Lord Beaverbrook asked, "How has it come about?" and he gave the following answer: "Through the leadership of Churchill, through the vision of the President, through the foresight of my own countryman Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada, through the heroic resistance of the British people and through the wave of comradeship and resistance they have awakened in the American nation".
It might be recalled that Lord Beaverbrook is at once a Canadian and a Conservative, and that tribute arose out of no personal partiality for the Prime Minister.
It might also be worth while to refer to the recognition of the Prime Minister's leadership of Canada expressed by two members of parliament who do not support the government. Senator A. D. McRae of Vancouver was reported by the Toronto Star of October 3, 1940, as follows:
Everybody feels that the government is making a tremendous effort. That is true of my province, where criticism was rampant before, and it struck me as evident everywhere I visited.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Han-sell) is reported by the Lethbridge Herald of October 31, 1940, as follows:
Referring to Prime Minister King, Mr. Hansel! said he believed the Prime Minister is handling the war effort admirably.
Therefore, of course, I cannot support the amendment.
We know that Canada, before and during the last war and pretty well ever since up to a certain time, was divided. Hon. members remember what happened, whether they give the Prime Minister credit or not; the king and his beautiful queen visited Canada, and I believe Montreal tried to outdo the great cities of Toronto and Fort William in manifestations of loyalty. A spirit of loyalty swept
[Mr. Mclvor.l
across our great country; there was unity then and since, and Canada has gone into the war with a united front. No prime minister in the history of Canada has done a greater deed. Therefore I shall vote against the amendment.
Then there is the unity of parliament in the declaration of war and in the prosecution of the war.
Thinking of the Prime Minister, I see him brought up in a Christian home where a man is expected to keep the Sabbath and to contribute of this world's goods for the needs of others. I refer hon. members to an article by George H. Lyon in a recent issue of the Evening Citizen. Hon. members would do well to read that article which is written by a citizen of the United States, showing the character of the Prime Minister as a man who is ready to serve the state before he serves himself.
Thinking of the government that supports the Prime Minister, I take off my hat to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), remembering that when there was a surplus of butter in Canada that could not be sold, he did what? He did not store it with the packers; he stored it in the relief departments of our cities, and we distributed: it freely to those in need.
In the new world order of which the Prime Minister speaks, I expect his government will support him through thick and thin. I say that because honour should be rendered to whom honour is due. Therefore, when I am asked to give a vote of want of confidence in this government, I have to satisfy my better judgment and my conscience; I believe the Prime Minister is worthy of our support, and I believe there are very few hon. members in this house who will not support him.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that you would expect me, nor would the house expect me, this evening to follow exactly the same line of argument as that pursued by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), strong and convincing as his arguments always are. In speaking to this amendment and the subamend-ment I shall try to deal with the difficulties of agriculture in Canada to-day in a fashion that I hope will not be regarded as an attempt at a critical extravaganza or, as some hon. members have, I think, attempted to deal with it, by putting one's head in the sand and taking a complacent attitude with regard to Canadian agricultural problems in general. It seems to me that- somewhere in between those two points of view lies the commonsense approach to the problem at the present time.

Supply-State of Agriculture
It appears to me, as I am sure it does to every member in this chamber to-night, that during this period, while the shadow of war lies across every legislative body, and every home and community of this dominion, it becomes incumbent upon each of us to deal with these problems in a manner which does not smack of an endeavour to gain some small party or political advantage. We should appreciate that we are here representing the men and women of our constituencies, and should be prepared to assist the government, in some constructive manner, by pointing out the problems with which agriculture is faced, putting up to the government fairly and squarely what we think should be done, and then leaving it to the government to take the necessary action.
I am sorry that hon. gentlemen opposite have taken the attitude that this is a mere want of confidence motion, and so they must vote against it. Those who hold that view have, I think, misunderstood the purpose of the amendment. We who are honestly trying to put forward the point of view of the farmers have no desire to overthrow the administration or to harass the government unduly. We readily understand that the government is sufficiently embarrassed when it has to face problems as broad, deep, serious and important as those now facing agriculture. I am sure we all appreciate the position in which the government finds itself. After all, however, experience has shown that unless we lay some emphasis on any proposal advanced and put some teeth into it, the government is apt to treat the whole problem as something not of paramount importance, and that is really the reason underlying the amendment which is under discussion to-night. I hope that by the time this debate concludes, the minister and the government will be so fully seized of the significance of the problem that something will be done. I hope that they will appreciate the various points of view advanced, and that when this debate is over, they will take steps materially to help agriculture on its way to better times.
I am one of those who believe that the problems now facing agriculture are not strictly the result of the war. It is true that they may have been accentuated and perhaps aggravated in some respects by the war. I would not deny that, but many times in years gone by hon. members have seriously and honestly asked the government if we could not have in Canada some sort of plan with regard to agriculture that might be followed through the years. I have listened, since I came to parliament, to many hon. members criticizing the government because of the way agricultural problems are faced. One of the major criticisms that I would advance in connection with this government-I cannot say with regard to previous governments, for I was not here-is with reference to the lack of any plan so far as agriculture in this country is concerned. When the war came on, the farming communities were so emaciated financially and economically, as a result of conditions which had existed previously, that they were much less able to withstand the rigours of a war effort than they should have been.
Of course attempts have been made in the past to develop a plan for the betterment of agriculture in this dominion. Whatever may have been its weaknesses, the Natural Products Marketing Act, which was passed in 1934, at least was a step in that direction. When that act was declared ultra vires by the privy council, after having been dealt with by the supreme court, I thought this government could very well have had the British North America Act amended, as was done with regard to unemployment insurance, in order to permit that legislation to remain in force, with such amendments as might be found necessary during the course of its operation. That, at all events, would have provided some sort of scheme or plan to assist agriculture, but that was not done.
As most hon. members realize, agriculture finds itself in a peculiar position. It has been said many times that thirty-five per cent of our population receive only nine per cent or eleven per cent of the national income. That is only too true. There are, however, some other points that I should like also to place before the house. According to the census of 1931, thirty-nine per cent of the population of Canada was rural, while sixty-one per cent was urban. That was a great change from 1871, when twenty-two per cent of the population was urban and seventy-eight per cent was rural. All through the years a steady drift from the farms to the urban centres has brought about this great change. In addition, the farmer is faced with the lack of many facilities that are possessed by people enjoying an ordinary standard of living. Perhaps it might not be out of place here to mention that, according to the last dominion census, in Ontario only one farm out of every ten had water piped into the kitchen; one farm out of every sixteen had a bathroom with water piped in; one farm out of every five had a radio, while one farm out of every six had electricity or gas. I must admit, of course, that this last figure has been somewhat changed in recent years.
Perhaps what I have said will give some picture of agricultural conditions. But may
Supply-State oj Agriculture

I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that while many, farm problems are of long standing, one of the most acute difficulties at the present time is brought about by the disparity in prices about which we have heard so much. The question of what the farmer has to pay and what he receives for his products is a matter of serious concern to every rural dweller in this dominion. The other day I saw some statistics comparing prices during the last war with prices during this war, and I noticed that as compared with February, 1916, total wholesale prices of Canadian farm products in February, 1941, showed a reduction of 18 per cent. This gives one some conception of problems the farmer faces now, in comparison with those he faced in those times. In addition to that, the difference between 1915 and 1940, so far as farm wages paid by fanners in Canada were concerned, showed a present-day increase of 50 per cent for male help and 48 per cent for female help over the 1915 figure. One can readily understand, therefore, that the problem of the farmer is not one which can be lightly brushed aside.
While I do not wish to be regarded as a demagogue in a matter of this kind, I should like to place on Hansard some comparative figures which will serve to place perhaps more clearly before lion, members the position in which the farmer finds himself when he goes to buy some of the things he requires.
[ have before me a table which I believe sets out clearly what I have in mind and, while 1 shall not read it all, I shall place one or two items on record.
Under present prices, when a farmer goes to buy a suit of clothes for himself he has to pay the equivalent of the present price of 100 bushels of oats. Two and a half acres of soil are required to grow those oats. Then, to make a further comparison, that suit of clothes would cost him the equivalent of the selling price of 100 pounds of butter. Or, if we may speak in terms of the time it takes a cow to produce the amount of butter required to buy the suit of clothes, we might say that the cow would have to work 146 days to produce the required amount.
We have heard a great deal of talk about man-hours. At this time I am going to say something about cow-hours. It takes 3,504 cow-hours for the good old dairy cow to produce enough butter to pay for the farmer's suit of clothes.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And what about the bull?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And it would take about 7,000 cow-hours to pay for the suit worn by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght), because his suit is a more expensive one.
[Mr. Graydon.1

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which side do you milk her from?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may be there are
some farmers in the house who do not know which side; but I know it, for I have sat on her right side a good many times.
At any rate, to return to the figures, the farmer must sell 600 bushels of oats if he wishes to have enough money to buy an electric refrigerator. He must sow fifteen acres of ground to produce those oats. Then, we find that it would take one cow 876 days to produce sufficient to pay for a refrigerator or, if we may again make the comparison by cow-hours, we find that 21,024 cow-hours are required.
When a farmer hires a man, paying him at the rate of 8700 a year-and that is not an unfair figure, when one considers board- he must sell 2,000 bushels of oats at present prices if he wishes to pay his helper's wages. Fifty acres of land would be required to produce those oats. Or, to make a further comparison, he would have to sell 2,000 pounds of butter, and it would take one cow eight years to produce to that value. In other words, those wages would have an equivalent of 70,080 cow-hours. I shall not place further figures on the record, because those I have given will be sufficient at least to show the position in which the farmer finds himself when he makes purchases.
When we speak about the problems connected with agriculture, and the remedies which could be applied, I am the first to admit that those problems are not easy to solve. There is no use in any hon. .member rising in his place in the house and saying that agricultural problems can be solved overnight. I am not suggesting that that be done. My disagreement, with the government's action is that I am not sure that a real plan has been put into effect to help agriculture; in fact, I am sure it has not.
Permit me to place on record an example which, while perhaps not entirely comparable, goes at least part way toward illustrating the point I wish to make. When Mr. Roosevelt brought down his war appropriation bill for seven billion dollars in March of this year, we find that that bill, passed by the United States congress, placed farm commodities second on the list, so far as government expenditures are concerned. Actually one dollar out of every five spent by Mr. Roosevelt is spent on the farmers in the United States. On the other hand, in our appropriation bill for $1,450,000,000 we allocated the magnificent sum of one dollar out of every $180 to the farmers of Canada. I bring these facts to the attention of the minister,

Supply-State of Agriculture
because I believe they are of some importance, and show the disparity between the manner in which farmers in the United States and those in Canada are treated. It shows, too, the way in which the respective governments regard the farmers, as an essential part of the war effort.
I would go one step farther in discussing the point as to how the government is meeting the problems of the farmers. I am sure the government could not have turned a deaf ear to farmers in Canada during the last few months, because those farmers have been fairly vocal, when placing their problems before governments and the people generally.
In view of these circumstances I was amazed to find what the records revealed. A committee on agriculture was set up by the house.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where is it?

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Someone asks, "Where is it?" Before I have finished, I will tell him where it has been the last while back. In 1936, the committee on agriculture sat to discuss farm implement prices. In 1937, a new, special committee dealt with the same subject. Then, in the same session, that committee sat not more than a few days to deal with two small bills which had reference to the sale of feeds, and regulations in connection therewith. In 1938, the committee sat for some considerable time on a measure to amend the Canada Grain Act. It sat again in 1939 to consider a further amendment to the Canada Grain Act, and to consider Bill No. 104, concerning stockyards, live stock and live stock products.
While those may have been the problems of earlier years, we have now arrived at a time when agriculture in Canada is facing problems more acute than were faced in any of those years. Yet, since the last general election in March, 1940, the government has not called together the committee on agriculture, except for purposes of organization and to elect a chairman. I would indict the administration on that point alone, because it seems to me that in view of the multitude of problems facing the farmers of Canada, it would surely not be too much to ask the government to call together the sixty members of the committee on agriculture, and to turn them loose on some of the problems facing our farmers. Let that committee see if it can do something toward formulating a definite plan. That is what I ask with regard to the committee on agriculture.
Members of parliament generally seem to be chafing to have something to do. They say there is no place fo" the private member. There is a place where in the last two sessions
of parliament sixty private members, with an intelligent outlook on agriculture, could have done something for that industry. Many of those members were fully qualified to bring to the solution of agricultural problems some of the best brains in Canada. The committee on agriculture should have had the opportunity to hear men representative of agriculture throughout Canada. From the evidence placed before the committee, it is possible it might have suggested something by way of a plan to remedy many of the difficulties facing agriculture at the present time.	[DOT]
Before I close my remarks I should like to make one or two suggestions to the government in addition to those which have been made already. I am prepared to acknowledge that in some lines of endeavour the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) seems to have done a pretty good job, but I am not so sure that it is in the line of agriculture. It seems to me that when the Department of National War Services required the services of a minister, the Department of Agriculture should not have been called upon to fill this need. If the Department of National War Services was important enough to warrant a full-time minister, the government should not have encroached upon the field of agriculture to obtain a minister. I feel sure that I voice the opinion of the farmers in my riding, and I believe the farmers in Ontario, when I say that the call now is for a full-time Minister of Agriculture. That call is insistent and incessant. This government will eventually have to wake up to the fact that there is a demand that the services of at least one farmer should be at the fulltime disposal of the Department of Agriculture here at Ottawa.
May I suggest to the minister, when he again takes over the portfolio of agriculture, that he should set up the committee on agriculture or appoint a special committee to study these matters. The farmers are asking that some evidence be produced that this government is really making an effort to solve their problems. The best brains of industry have been brought to Ottawa in order to solve the problems faced by other departments, but so far as I have been able to find out, this government has not taken the trouble to bring to Ottawa many representatives of the farmers in order that their problems may be tackled in the proper way. The problems being faced by the Department of Munitions and Supply, the Department of National Defence and other departments are important, so far as our war effort is concerned, but so are those faced by the Department of Agriculture. Representative men should be brought here in order that their
Supply-State of Agriculture

views may be had with regard to the solution of the problems which confront the farming population.
I see no reason why farming and labouring men should not be appointed to many of the departmental boards which have been set up. The question will be asked: What do they know about these problems? We have a tendency, I fear, in this house to get away from the viewpoint of the workingman and the farmer. I should like to see many more bona fide workingmen and farmers brought to Ottawa to help in the solution of our national problems. They would be able to bring to these matters a common sense, practical viewpoint, sometimes not possessed by others of our citizens who are lauded so highly with respect to the contribution that they are making. I believe such workingmen and farmers would bring a new light to bear upon the multitudinous problems which face our country to-day.
I do not think farm products are advertised to-day as widely and as effectively as they should be. Sometimes I think we pay almost as much for the containers of certain manufactured goods as we do for the product itself. It does not seem to me right that our farm products should not be as well advertised as our manufactured products. I have been told by advertising men-and I think they are correct-that it is advertising that largely sells a product. They say that if you put a fair product in a nice package and advertise it effectively, it will sell. But these methods do not appear to be used as fully as they should be so far as our farm products are concerned.
In this connection I wish to commend the government for the move they have made in connection with apples and apple juice. The market in Great Britain for apples was lost some time ago. Two years ago no hon. member would think of asking for apple juice; he might know something about hard cider but not about apple juice. To-day I suppose that as much apple juice is consumed at the breakfast tables of Canada as is any other delectable drink with which a meal could be started. This is all due to the effect of advertising. There is no reason why the government could not do the same thing in connection with many other farm products.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I assure my hon. friend that I give him full credit for advertising apple juice. If he wants it more clearly, I make this public declaration that the Minister of Agriculture is responsible for every glass of apple juice to be found on the tables of Canadian homes. We like to give credit where credit is due. I know the minister with his modest manner would prefer that I make the statement rather than he.
Despite the explanation which the minister has attempted to make with regard to the feeble-I say that advisedly-advertising campaign in connection with some agricultural products, there is not one farmer in Canada who thinks that this advertising campaign to sell the average farm product is sufficiently effective at the moment. If the minister can do as good a job with other farm products as he has done with apple juice, I am sure the farmers of Canada will be well satisfied.
I am hopeful that something concrete will be done with respect to organized farming. Most of us who have come off the farm realize the difficulties faced by agriculture. This industry is not organized, but it has to deal with other industries which are highly organized, and many of our difficulties arise in that connection.
I am sure that we are all anxious to see the farming industry throughout Canada speak with one voice instead of with many voices as it has done in the past. I take the word of one of the main speakers at the annual meeting of the Canadian federation of agriculture which I attended in Toronto not many months ago, who said that some responsibility rests on the agriculture industry itself as well as on the government. I certainly would not go the length of saying that the whole responsibility must rest upon the government, but rather I would say that an organized agriculture should work in cooperation with the government; and with the two working hand in hand, plans can be formulated and put into action from which good results may reasonably be expected. Many people look

Supply-State oj Agriculture
upon agricultural problems as problems of a domestic nature only, but in fact our farm problems are related to our whole war effort. Let us never at any time minimize the importance of the production of foodstuffs in the winning of this war.
May I say to the minister who has brought down this policy of reducing the acreage in production that the considered opinion of most of the farmers with whom I have spoken is that we shall live to rue the day when we reduced the productive capacity of the farms of Canada. That view may be entirely wrong, but it is the view nevertheless of most agriculturists. I say, further, I am convinced that, as time goes on, we shall have a greater need of foodstuffs than ever before, and it will not be easy to travel back over the road once we have taken the wrong turn, because agriculture must make its plans years ahead.
We are planning now for a reduction of acreage in western Canada and for a reduction in the production of certain types of grain. The fear of the eastern farmer is that this policy means not only the curtailing of acreage in western Canada but bringing into competition with the eastern agriculturist many factors with which he has not hitherto had to compete. Whether that be true or not, I think the Minister of Agriculture might well give consideration to this point of view, that he is really asking the agriculturists of eastern Canada to pay a high price for the benefits which are going to western Canada, a higher price than the eastern agriculturists should properly be called upon to pay. If we are going to help the agriculturists of western Canada-and I am one of those who believe that we should help them-western agriculture should be helped out of the purse of Canada as a whole, and not so largely at the expense of eastern agriculture. Many farmers in my part of the country have felt throughout the years that the eastern farmer has been the forgotten man, and in many respects, Mr. Speaker, I believe that he has been the forgotten man. It is time now, if it is not too late, to formulate and bring down some plan for bringing back this war-time industry of agriculture to a position where we can see in the future something approaching a fair parity of prices, a policy that will give a fair and square and just deal to the man who makes his living from the soil.
I should like to close by quoting one sentence taken from one of the farm papers which I have had the pleasure of reading almost ever since I was a child, The Farmers' Advocate. This sentence, which appears in its issue of January 9, 1941, I think pretty well sums up the feeling which I know the average farmer to entertain. It says:
If this is an all-out total war, let it be one with the burden falling on all classes. Then the man at the desk, at the bench, in the counting house, or at the plough, will feel that he is not being exploited, and will gladly give his time and talent in the cause of liberty, equity and justice.

maintopic: AGRICULTURE-AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset offer my congratulations and compliments to the previous speaker (Mr. Graydon). On both sides of the house we have always found him an interesting speaker, and his moderation and sound reasoning have always appealed to the house. While I cannot agree with everything he has said, he made one statement which I was very glad to hear, namely, that the amendment we are discussing this evening was not brought forward in an attempt to overthrow the government, but was rather, to use his own words, for the purpose of formulating an amendment which would have a little teeth in it, the views of hon. gentlemen opposite. It so happens that, as the amendment is worded, it has not only teeth but quite a kick in it.
I feel, as does the hon. member for Peel, that the discussion of this important subject of agriculture would have been on a much higher plane had it not been brought up in the form of a want of confidence motion. The suggestion which my hon. friend has made that many of these agricultural problems should be referred to the committee on agriculture is one that should be given consideration. I believe that such a procedure would assist us in planning a solution which often we find it difficult to achieve in the house. For example, as we all know, the wheat problem has been discussed lengthily in this chamber, and rightly so, because the producer of wheat really has a problem on his hands. But if the greater part of the discussion that has taken place on wheat had taken place in the committee on agriculture, I believe that the business of parliament would have been expedited and perhaps it would have been easier to find a solution.
Coming from a dairy section of the country, I should like to speak of dairy farming in general, and in particular of the butter producer. I do not know that I shall have anything new to offer in the remarks I intend to make, but it is a human trait, I believe, to reiterate the different views which interest us. One of the things we in the eastern townships are particularly interested in is dairying, and especially the production of butter. Year after year since 1932, if not before, our dairy farmers have been living in hopes that their lot would be alleviated, and although it must be admitted that certain legislation has been passed which helped
Supply-State of Agriculture

It has been stated during the discussion on agriculture that the index price for receipts from the sale of farm products in 1940, as compared with the returns for 1926 to 1929, prove to us that the wheat-growing areas have suffered to a greater extent than any other agricultural areas. I should like at this time to place on record not index prices, but actual prices for wheat and butter in the last eight years, together with the attendant loss or gain, compared with prices of production of both of these commodities. For the basis of my comparison I shall take, as the price of producing wheat, the price set by the Saskatchewan legislature in February,
when it recommended that a minimum price of 85 cents, Fort William, should be set on wheat. Surely, if this enormous amount were needed to take care of the wheat industry, let us not bemoan or begrudge the small amount, comparatively speaking, of financial assistance the dairy industry needs to carry on, particularly in view of the meagre amounts which have been meted out to it.
